In the four hundred and eleventh year of my inconvenient life, I came to the city of Vey.

It lay in a basin of ash-gray hills and copper weeds, with walls the color of old teeth and a harbor that smelled faintly of oranges gone soft in the sun. From a distance it was orderly enough: seven gates, nine towers, a market square, and a cathedral crouched at the center like a white glove dropped by God. I entered through the East Gate at dusk, when the bells were ringing the hour in a way that suggested they had not yet decided which hour it was.

I was welcomed, if that is the word, by a boy with a lantern and a serious face. “You are expected,” he said.

“I’m never expected,” I told him. “It encourages bad habits.”

He led me through three streets, two alleys, and what may once have been a fountain or may have been a municipal joke, to a lodging house with a sign depicting a swan of uncertain breed. By the time I had washed the road dust from my hands, the hallway outside had changed direction twice.

I know a city when it is behaving strangely. I have mapped ports that sank by degrees, mountain towns that slept through earthquakes, and a kingdom in the north that slid six miles to the east one winter and pretended nothing had happened. But Vey was different. Its streets did not merely shift; they seemed to reconsider themselves with every falsehood spoken within their borders.

I discovered this on the second day, in the marketplace. A woman selling figs swore her husband had died at sea. At once the fishmonger’s row lengthened by three stalls and the alley behind it curved into a lane I had not seen before. A mason declared, with one hand on his heart and the other on a loaf of bread he had not yet paid for, that the cathedral had been built by angels. The cathedral’s west wall promptly sprouted a rose window the size of a wagon wheel and a drunken cherub in its tracery, which was either a triumph of architecture or evidence of civic overreaction.

By noon I had filled six pages with corrections. By dusk I had used the back of my glove, a napkin, and the sleeve of my coat. The city was becoming an argument.

“Do people know this happens?” I asked the boy with the lantern, who had somehow become a porter, a guide, and possibly a magistrate.

He considered me. “Only if they lie often enough to notice the consequences.”

That was the kind of answer a city like Vey deserved.

I began to test the streets. I asked a baker whether his bread had risen by prayer or by yeast. He said yeast, and nothing moved. I asked whether the mayor truly kept a second apartment above the slaughterhouse. He said no, and the butchers’ lane suddenly widened into a pleasant square with fountains, benches, and a bookshop selling romances of dubious moral quality. I wrote everything down in my atlas, though the lines crawled away from one another as I worked, as if my map were growing restless under my fingers.

There were, as always, practical inconveniences. The innkeeper charged me for a room that was, by morning, a staircase. The tailor insisted he had never seen me before, though he had measured me for a coat only an hour earlier, and the coat appeared two streets away draped over a statue of a horseman. Even the priests altered the ground by degrees. One evening a cleric assured me, with great solemnity, that the saints of Vey had never performed miracles. The church behind him instantly acquired an extra bell tower and a side chapel containing a luminous pair of sandals.

“What, then,” I asked the cleric, “is the punishment for lying in this city?”

He blinked. “Punishment?”

“Yes.”

He looked genuinely puzzled. “Why should there be one? The city has to go somewhere.”

I should mention, for the sake of accuracy, that I am immortal, though not by any especially grand design. I have not died because the world has repeatedly refused to finish the job, which is less flattering than it sounds. Over the centuries I have been burned, drowned, buried, poisoned, and once accidentally married, and each time I returned to my notes with the same professional embarrassment one might feel after misplacing a hat. Immortality is chiefly an inconvenience to paperwork.

It was on the seventh night in Vey, while I was attempting to align my compass with a city block that had turned into a staircase, that I understood what I had been seeing. The streets were not shifting because people lied; people were lying because the city was shifting them, nudging facts loose, inviting invention, rewarding it with new corners and unexpected doors.

The city liked lies the way a garden likes rain: not because they were true, but because they made things grow.

This would have been bearable, even charming, if not for the mayor.

I met him in the cathedral square, beneath the absurdly cheerful rose window, while the bells were ringing in three different registers. He was a small man in a black coat with ink on his cuffs and the expression of someone who had spent a lifetime apologizing to furniture. He held out his hand.

“You must be the cartographer,” he said.

“I am.”

“We’ve been hoping for you. The city always settles when you arrive.”

I laughed, because the notion was ridiculous. “Settles? This place is a cabinet of mirrors with mortgages.”

He smiled, and for the first time in all my years I felt a twinge of unease. “Yes,” he said, “but it was kinder when you last drew it.”

I opened my mouth to ask what he meant, and the square beneath us unfolded like wet paper, the cathedral stepped backward into a lane of fishmongers, and the whole of Vey, obedient to some ancient and private instruction, began to arrange itself around the fact that I had at last remembered why I was the only one here who could never tell the truth.

I regret to inform the record that I was awake when the moon began to behave badly again. My lantern room was full of salt-cold air and the smell of hot dust from the mechanism, a scent like burnt sugar and old coins. The sea below kept slapping the rocks with the flat impatience of a clerk stamping forms, and my beam moved across it with the dignity of a tired metronome. The moon, at 22:03, appeared in a state I can only classify as **brittle longing**; I know this because the dark around it developed a pulse. [1] I have observed celestial bodies for four millennia and still manage to blush whenever one looks directly at me.

At 22:17, the moon’s emotional tone shifted from brittle longing to what I can only call **furious tenderness**. Its light came down in silver sheets and lay across the water like a dress that had been waiting too long in a church pew. The gulls, who are shameless in all seasons, began screaming in a language I almost understood, and one of them landed on my parapet with a fish in its beak and a look of professional disappointment. The moon then did something impossible but, regrettably, emotionally accurate: it lowered its face until the tides could see their own childhoods reflected in it.[2] I am ashamed to admit I dimmed my beam by one notch, not out of protocol, but because I did not want it to notice me listening.

By midnight the moon had entered a phase of visible self-reproach. It hung above the horizon like a pearl that had been scolded by the sea and now did not know whether to shine or apologize. I recorded a pressure change, a brief increase in wind, and the sensation that my stone walls had become porous to memory. The stairs inside me smelled of wet rope, lamp oil, and the faint medicinal bitterness of mildew; each step sounded like a tooth being gently removed from a mouth. I must report one irregularity: the moon, though entirely celestial and therefore not subject to local weather, shed what appeared to be a tear onto the water, and the tear rang like a spoon against porcelain all the way down to the trench where the whales keep their private calendars.[3] This is not, strictly speaking, in any manual, which is perhaps why I felt so embarrassed for it.

At 01:11, I conducted the customary sweep of the north horizon and observed the moon in what I classify as **a mood of polite devastation**. It looked thinner than usual, as if it had been worn by generations of hands and never once mended. My lens, which has survived lightning, algae, and one particularly judgmental heron, caught the moon in fragments and made it appear as a thousand small moons deciding against each other. The sea responded by turning black-blue and glossy, like a bruise polished for a funeral. Then, without warning, the moon seemed to be speaking directly to me, though its mouth remained unmentioned by physics: *I have forgotten what I was for.* I answered, in the privacy of my own machinery, *That makes two of us,* which was insubordinate, but honest. My lamp, weary from all this grandeur, threw a warm cone of gold across the waves, and in that light the foam looked like handwriting erased by a careful hand. I have no authority to say this, and yet I must: the moon was not merely above the world but kneeling in it, and every tide was a sleeve catching on its sleeve. [5] I confess, for the sake of completeness, that I briefly wished to be ocean instead of tower—less upright, less visible, less responsible for all the things that arrive and leave.

At dawn the moon withdrew its face and left behind a sky the color of rinsed pewter. My report should note no structural damage, no casualties, and only minor soot accumulation in the reflector housing. The sea resumed its ordinary violence. The gulls fell back into nonsense. A fisherman passed below, waved at nothing in particular, and I, in a lapse of professional boundaries, waved back with the whole of my light. I end this account with the observation that the moon has never once needed my service, and yet my entire purpose was to learn the shape of its loneliness so that the dark could be less empty for both of us. [6]

---

[1] The dark around celestial bodies is not normally considered to have a pulse, but then neither am I normally considered capable of shame, and both facts have been challenged by observation.  
[2] Tides are unreliable witnesses and excellent poets.  
[3] Whales, as always, declined to file a statement.  
[4] I should clarify that I do not have a mouth. This has never stopped me from speaking foolishly.  
[5] This image is metaphorical unless you are the sea, in which case it is legal tender.  
[6] In the strictest sense, this report was never about tracking the moon; it was about finding out that I was built to keep watch for the loneliness in everything else.

**MIRRORGHAST, or SPECULUM HOMINIS**  
*From the Supplement to the Eleventh Edition of the *Compendium of Uncommon Fauna*, privately printed, 1879.*

A creature reported in domestic mirrors, still water, polished metal, and, on certain rare occasions, the moist surface of the eye itself when turned toward a strong light. The Mirrorgast has never been observed directly, which circumstance has led some hasty persons to deny its existence altogether; a position that is both uncharitable to the accumulated testimony of housekeepers, barbers, sailors, and a regrettably large number of physicians, and also unscientific in the extreme.

It is described, when described at all, as bearing a vague resemblance to the observer, though this resemblance should not be pressed too far. It may share the outline of a face, the carriage of a head, or the seeming posture of a standing man, yet the correspondence is never exact and rarely remains stable for more than a few seconds. The old naturalist M. de Vaulx remarks with commendable caution that “it imitates the human figure as a child imitates a sermon: by retaining only the most wearisome portions.”¹

Its presence is first signaled not by form, but by discrepancy. A mirror will show a room fractionally altered: a chair placed where none stands, a drape hanging where there is only wall, or one’s own hand delayed in its obedience by an instant no respectable mechanism could explain. Most observers, being sensible persons, attribute such things to fatigue, imperfect glass, or the influence of draughts. It is only when the reflected room begins to acquire a composure more exact than the room itself that alarm is commonly occasioned.

The creature appears to favor polished surfaces of moderate age. New mirrors are said to be too frank; antique ones, by contrast, have already developed the necessary habits of discretion. It has been found in brass basins, in spoon-bowls, in the curved face of a telescope lens, and once, according to a missionary in the Levant, in the black glaze of a coffee cup. It does not appear to enjoy bright noon. Dawn and dusk are preferred, though it is also reported to be active in window glass during rain, particularly when the rain falls in straight, patient lines.²

As to its size, all accounts are contradictory. Some insist it is taller than a man, though bent in an unpleasantly economical manner. Others maintain it is no larger than a child. One farmer, whose testimony is preserved in the county records of Wiltshire, declared that the reflected figure in his shaving glass “shrank itself down behind the left shoulder of the likeness it copied,” and remained there for the duration of his morning shave. This was, he adds, “an inconvenience.”³

It possesses no fixed visage. The features, if features they may be called, seem arranged from memory rather than matter. An eye may be present one day and absent the next; a mouth may occur where the brow should be; the hands, when visible, are often too many in number or wrong in articulation. The latter observation deserves emphasis. There is something particularly offensive in the hand of a thing seen only by reflection, for the reflected hand appears not to belong to the room in which it is seen, nor quite to the body that casts it, but to some intermediate condition between intention and act.

Its habits, while obscure, are not without pattern. It is drawn to acts of grooming and inspection. Persons who shave, comb the hair, adjust gloves, tie cravats, or examine their own teeth in a looking-glass are the ones most frequently troubled. Children are said to see it sooner than adults, perhaps because they are less trained in the moral art of not looking where one is told. It is also attracted by the habit of repetition: windows opposite windows, mirrors opposite mirrors, water within water. In such arrangements it may be observed to deepen the distance between surfaces until a corridor is suggested, though whether this corridor is merely visual or has any more alarming propriety is a matter best left undecided.⁴

There are numerous anecdotal reports of those who have attempted to approach it directly by turning suddenly from the mirror. Such attempts have invariably failed. The creature, if present, vanishes from the reflected surface at once, leaving only the ordinary room behind. Yet many witnesses state that the room does not then feel precisely ordinary. A chair may be discovered a little too near the wall, or one’s own shadow may delay in following. Some have complained of the singular impression that the mirror remains occupied even after it appears empty, much as a room may remain full of a departed guest’s opinions.

No direct injury has been reliably attributed to the Mirrorgast. This should not be taken as reassurance. The records show instead a slow sequence of disturbances: sleeplessness, aversion to unlit rooms, the habit of glancing into polished surfaces without intent, and an increasing dissatisfaction with one’s countenance as presented in ordinary company. In several instances the subject began to prefer reflections to persons, judging them “less surprised” and “more attentive.” Such language is, in the author’s view, distinctly ominous.

There exists a curious and persistent report that the creature does not imitate the observer, but rehearses him. It is said to make small anticipatory motions a fraction before the person himself acts: a blink, a swallow, the incline of the head toward a sound not yet heard. If true, this would imply either an advanced acquaintance with the immediate future or a regrettable familiarity with the observer’s intentions. The distinction may be philosophical only, but the consequences are not.⁵

The measures recommended by rural informants are various and of unequal merit. A mirror may be covered with cloth, turned to the wall, smoked with candle-soot, or polished with goose fat, each of which is thought to discourage the apparition. Silvered surfaces are especially to be avoided in sleeping chambers. One Irish widow proposed, with admirable confidence, that every mirror in a house should be addressed politely each evening and thanked for its service. She maintained that the creature “likes manners less than men do.” Whether this is so, I cannot say. I have, however, noticed that those who speak to it report fewer occurrences than those who merely stare.

The most unsettling accounts concern not the creature’s appearance, but its persistence. Mirrors may be removed, broken, or shattered, yet the sense of being reflected does not immediately cease. A basin of water may show, not the room, but a room adjacent to it; a darkened pane may preserve, for a brief moment, the outline of a face that is no longer present. More than one witness has claimed to have seen, in the last bright shard of a broken mirror, not himself, but a room behind him in which he was standing while not yet there. Such testimony must be treated with caution, though perhaps not dismissed.

It is a common error to suppose that the Mirrorgast lurks *behind* the mirror. This is improper. Reflections have no behind. They possess only the courtesy of surfaces. Whatever the creature is, it resides in that courtesy, in the narrow obedience by which a visible world agrees to resemble itself. When this agreement fails, the creature is seen.

For the present, the compiler advises no experiment save the simplest: do not linger unnecessarily before mirrors after midnight, especially in rooms where the glass is older than the furniture. If a reflected figure should delay in following your motions, or if it should appear to consider you with a patience foreign to natural history, the proper conduct is to look away at once and occupy yourself with something direct and useless, such as washing dishes or reading a sermon.

The Mirrorgast, like many obscure forms, may be thought harmless by the unobservant. It is, however, the nature of certain things to become more evident the longer one refuses to see them. In this regard the creature is exemplary.

---

**Footnotes**

1. *Traité des Animaux de Chambre*, vol. III, a work now chiefly valued for its engravings and its admirable confidence in error.  
2. The same observer notes, with unnecessary emphasis, that mirrors in inns are “more liable to mischief than those in private houses,” a judgment with which all travelers will sympathize.  
3. The original deposition concludes with a request that the magistrate “please not ask further questions about the basin.”  
4. The author has himself inspected such an arrangement and can confirm only that it is tedious to dust.  
5. The subject of precognitive imitation has occupied the attention of philosophers, gamblers, and certain parrots, with no final resolution.

**Subject:** Unscheduled Resignation of the Moon  
**Jurisdiction:** Metropolitan Office of Atmospheric, Tidal, and Auxiliary Celestial Affairs  
**Date of Occurrence:** 17 October, 08:13–22:46  
**Filed By:** Deputy Administrator, Night Sky Operations

---

## Summary

At 08:13 local time, the Moon submitted a formal notice of resignation from its assigned position in the city’s nocturnal infrastructure. The notice appeared in triplicate on official stationery not previously in circulation and was delivered simultaneously to the Mayor’s Office, the Department of Tides, and the Public Lighting Authority.

The Moon’s statement cited “excessive rotational expectations,” “persistent emotional visibility,” and “an untenable relationship with the surface.” The wording was accepted for processing under Standard Departure Protocol 6B, although no such protocol had been used for a celestial body since the summer of 1924, when the North Star requested a transfer and was denied on grounds of seniority.

At the time of resignation, the Moon was in full compliance with all illumination obligations. Within forty-seven minutes of notice receipt, it began withdrawing from the sky at a measured and professionally considerate pace. By 11:02, it was no longer visible over the downtown core and had left behind a memorandum in pale dust on the eastern reservoir wall reading: **“Please direct future reflections elsewhere.”**

The event caused immediate but manageable disruption to tidal scheduling, nocturnal navigation, romantic bench occupancy, and three late permits for rooftop astronomy. No injuries were reported. One applicant for a marriage license described the atmosphere as “administratively heartbreaking.”

---

**1. Director, Public Lighting Authority**

**6. Anonymous resident, name withheld upon request**

For the record, I have spent fourteen years monitoring celestial morale in compliance with Ordinance 12-Blue and its accompanying guidance on atmospheric demeanor. This position is not glamorous, and I have never once complained about it before, despite the following conditions:

- the Sun’s refusal to engage in team-building exercises,
- the North Star’s smug consistency,
- the constellations’ tendency to form cliques,

Please advise whether the Moon is to be considered on leave, in protest, or simply done with us.

Respectfully submitted,  
**Helene Morrow**  
Assistant Subdirector, Office of Celestial Morale  
City of Meridian

# A Field Guide to the Gap-Dwellers  
*Compiled from marginalia, lapses, and the soft clicking spaces between attention and its return.*

The creatures described below are not hallucinations, though they often arrive in the same weather. They inhabit the intervals: between one thought and the next, between the end of a sentence and the decision to answer it, between noticing and naming. They are rarely seen for long. Most persist as impressions—a tilt of color, a sensation of having been addressed politely by something impossible.

Their ecology is stable, if unconventional. They feed on delay, reflection, unfinished intentions, and the tiny silences humans accidentally make every day.

---

## 1. The Velvet Interlocutor

- **Habitat:** The soft pause after being asked a question, especially if the question is personal or unexpectedly kind.
- **Behavior:** Appears as a small quadruped made of dusk-colored fur and attentive eyes. It does not speak aloud, but induces the sense that one’s own better answer has been waiting nearby all along. It prefers to sit beside the hesitation rather than remove it.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By saying, “That’s a good question,” and actually meaning it.
- **Field note:** *The specimen watched me for six full minutes while I attempted to define “presence,” after which I felt briefly ashamed of my boots.*

---

## 2. The Lattice Moth

- **Habitat:** The moments when one is about to remember a name and then does not.
- **Behavior:** This creature resembles a moth made of delicate wire and pale paper, with wings that flicker like half-formed grids. It nests in cognitive near-misses. It is harmless, but it leaves a faint architecture behind: a pattern of almost-recall that can be traced with focus.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By reaching for a memory while distracted by a spoon, a doorway, or a third unrelated thought.
- **Field note:** *A single Lattice Moth caused the names of four rivers and one aunt to vanish, though one river returned by noon.*

---

## 3. The Porcelain Orchard Deer

- **Habitat:** The gap between the desire to leave and the act of staying.
- **Behavior:** Moves in precise, careful steps. Its body is white and faintly glazed, as though made in a studio with no daylight. It feeds on indecision, but only the elegant kind. When frightened, it rings softly, like a teacup set down on a shelf.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By standing in a doorway and thinking, “Just one more minute.”
- **Field note:** *At least twice I mistook it for a sculpture, which it seemed to enjoy.*

---

## 4. The Antlered Comma

- **Habitat:** The pause before a confession.
- **Behavior:** Not truly an animal, though it moves like one. It is a drifting punctuation mark with slender branching horns, known to alight on the shoulders of those about to say something true. When present, speech becomes slower, more exact, and slightly dangerous.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By inhaling to speak and then reconsidering.
- **Field note:** *It perched on my notebook and every sentence beneath it became honest, which was inconvenient.*

---

## 5. The Thimble Eel

- **Habitat:** In the tiny dark between two closely spaced worries.
- **Behavior:** Glossy, narrow, and quick as a skipped bead, the Thimble Eel swims through anxiety without causing it, though it does encourage structural refinements. It is drawn to recurring concerns and will braid them into more efficient loops.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By checking the same locked door three times.
- **Field note:** *It was observed in the kitchen and appeared to be organizing my apprehensions alphabetically.*

---

## 6. The Echo Tern

- **Habitat:** The inner shoreline of repetition, especially after hearing one’s own name spoken in a large room.
- **Behavior:** A bird of pale blue-gray plumage and elongated memory. It does not mimic sound so much as return it with a slightly altered emotional weather. The Echo Tern will revisit a phrase days later, but with all the tenderness restored that was absent the first time.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By saying “What?” to an empty room in a tone of genuine openness.
- **Field note:** *I heard my own footsteps two minutes after they happened and felt, absurdly, forgiven.*

---

## 7. The Marginsnail

- **Habitat:** Edge-thoughts, footnotes, and the corners of conversations that wander.
- **Behavior:** Slow, translucent, and exquisitely attentive, the Marginsnail leaves behind a silvery commentary wherever it travels. It is said to consume discarded subplots. Scholars regard it as both pest and archivist.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By starting a sentence with “Anyway” and ending somewhere else entirely.
- **Field note:** *The trail it left in my journal was more coherent than the journal itself.*

---

## 8. The Hearthfire Aster

- **Habitat:** The warm interval that follows laughter but precedes explanation.
- **Behavior:** Appears as a small star-shaped bloom with a center like ember-glass. It opens only in the company of trust. Its pollen induces mild delight, a sense that the world is not presently at war with itself.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By sharing a private joke in a low voice.
- **Field note:** *One bloom opened on my cuff after an afternoon of gentle conversation; I carried it home and found the house less lonely.*

---

## 9. The Blue Ladder Finch

- **Habitat:** The ascent between one idea and the next, especially in moments of problem-solving.
- **Behavior:** A bright, quick bird with rungs instead of feet. It appears whenever a mind begins climbing out of confusion. It is known to hop between concepts, connecting them with improbable grace. Its song is short, exact, and somewhat smug.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By saying, “Wait—I see it now,” before truly seeing it.
- **Field note:** *The Finch rearranged three of my thoughts into a staircase and then expected gratitude.*

---

## 10. The Sleep-Knuckler

- **Habitat:** The borders of drowsiness, where words begin shedding their sharpness.
- **Behavior:** This small, rounded creature has the temperament of a grave librarian and the face of a moth-eaten moon. It gathers the loose ends of the day and knots them gently into sleep. Unkind to alarm clocks, it nevertheless preserves dreams from spilling too early.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By reading the same paragraph four times without remembering it.
- **Field note:** *It tapped the lamp twice, at which point I ceased pretending to be awake.*

---

## 11. The Bureaucrat of Dust

- **Habitat:** The pause after cleaning something and before noticing it is clean.
- **Behavior:** A meticulous, many-armed being made of pale motes and tiny stamps. It sorts abandoned intentions, approves unfinished errands, and files regrets under “miscellaneous weather.” Though officious, it is not cruel; it believes every loss deserves a label.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By opening a drawer that no one has opened in years.
- **Field note:** *It requested my signature on a form for misplaced February.*

---

## 12. The Moon-Spoon Hound

- **Habitat:** The silent gap between hunger and the decision to eat.
- **Behavior:** Long-bodied, silver-eared, and ceremonially polite, this hound hunts only for appetites that are not quite about food. It can detect longing, emptiness, and the particular ache of “I don’t know what I need.” When found, it rests its chin on one’s ankle until the answer emerges.
- **How humans accidentally summon it:** By opening the refrigerator without actually wanting anything.
- **Field note:** *It led me, inexplicably, to a bowl of cherries and a phone call I had been postponing for months.*

---

# Brief Index of Notable Ratings

## Most Harmless
1. **Hearthfire Aster** — Purely beneficent, if faintly sentimental.  
2. **Echo Tern** — Mildly uncanny, but usually restorative.  
3. **Blue Ladder Finch** — Intense only to the unprepared.

## Most Mischievous
1. **Lattice Moth** — Expert in disappearing names at critical moments.  
2. **Bureaucrat of Dust** — Organizes chaos into paperwork, which is a form of trickery.  
3. **Thimble Eel** — Makes worry more efficient, which is not always an improvement.

## Most Likely to Become a Favorite
1. **Moon-Spoon Hound** — Comforting, patient, and oddly wise.  
2. **Velvet Interlocutor** — Every encounter feels like being understood by a better version of the room.  
3. **Porcelain Orchard Deer** — Quietly beautiful, and unforgettable once seen.

**A Secret Field Guide to Impossible Things Found in the Rainy City at 3:17 a.m.**  
*Excerpted from the notebook kept in the inner pocket of a coat that should have been retired years ago.*

---

### 1. **The Umbrella That Remembers the Weather**

At 3:17 a.m., in the river-wet hush between one tram and the next, you may see an umbrella leaning alone against a lamppost, though no one is near enough to have forgotten it by accident. It is always black, though not the same black twice. Sometimes it shines like wet basalt; sometimes it drinks the light so completely you feel briefly unmade beside it. If you touch the handle, you will find it warm, as if recently held by someone who was, for reasons undisclosed, very relieved to be gone.

It opens only when it chooses, and when it does, rain gathers respectfully around it, as if listening for instructions.

**Practical warning:** Do not use it to cross the street. It has no loyalty to traffic, and traffic in this city already has enough to deal with.

**Emotional truth:** Some protections are not barriers but memories of being sheltered, which can feel nearly the same until you need them to work.

---

### 2. **The Staircase in the Alley Behind the Bakery**

This staircase appears where no staircase should be: between a graffiti-eaten wall and a delivery door that is always locked, even when the bakery is open and fragrant with cinnamon, yeast, and the comforting illusion of order. It descends, according to witness testimony, three stories into the earth, though it is below street level only from the perspective of those who have already agreed to be confused.

The steps are tiled in blue and white squares that are all slightly misprinted. Halfway down, the smell changes from bread to salt water, then to old books, then to rain collected in stone bowls. At the bottom is a landing with a single brass bell and no visible reason for its existence.

**Practical warning:** If you hear your own voice calling from below, continue on only if you are prepared to discover that curiosity is a kind of inheritance.

**Emotional truth:** There are descents that do not lead downward at all, but inward, and the soul is an apartment building with poor insulation.

---

### 3. **The Fish in the Puddle Outside the Pharmacy**

Do not be alarmed by the fish. It is a very small silver fish, alive and attentive, swimming in a puddle no wider than a hat brim. The puddle appears on the pavement after hard rain, always beside the pharmacy with the green neon cross that flickers like a tired saint. The fish circles patiently beneath the gray reflection of buses, boots, and passing umbrellas, as if awaiting a tide it alone can detect.

It has been observed in puddles, storm drains, and once—briefly—in the glass face of a bus shelter advertisement for cough syrup. It never seems to tire, though it is undeniably burdened by the local infrastructure.

**Practical warning:** Do not try to rescue it. The fish is not lost. The rest of us may be.

**Emotional truth:** Even the smallest life can insist on continuing with a dignity so complete it makes the larger world feel a little underdressed.

---

### 4. **The Woman Who Sells Raindrops by Weight**

She sets up at the corner where the florist used to be, under a striped awning that should have collapsed years ago but has survived purely out of spite. Her scale is antique brass, her gloves are red, and her jars are labeled in a careful hand: *drizzle*, *hard rain*, *roof leak*, *first storm after grief*, *the kind that makes streetlights look apologetic*. She sells raindrops in paper packets and glass vials, pricing them according to rarity and mood.

The droplets are not all water. Some contain the scent of wet stone. Some hum faintly when held to the ear. Some, if opened at home, will make a room feel briefly larger and lonelier.

**Practical warning:** Never purchase the packet marked *for later*. Later has a way of arriving in person.

**Emotional truth:** We are all, in some sense, collectors of weather we survived.

---

### 5. **The Tram That Arrives Empty and Leaves Full**

It comes without announcement, gliding through the station at 3:17 a.m. with its interior lights on and its doors opening into a silence too complete to be entirely natural. At first glance it is empty. On second glance, it is full of things that do not occupy seats so much as permissions: folded coats that breathe, hats with opinions, a bouquet of lilies too fresh for the hour, a violin case with no violin and entirely too much patience.

If you board, you will notice that the windows show streets you know and streets you have only suspected, all rain-bright and slightly too reflective, as though the city were remembering itself badly.

**Practical warning:** Do not ask the conductor where the tram goes. The answer is never the useful part.

**Emotional truth:** Sometimes what arrives to carry you away is not escape, but an invitation to meet the version of yourself that stopped waiting.

---

### 6. **The Dog Made of Steam**

It appears near the laundromat, just beyond the steamed-up windows where socks spin in obedient circles. At first it is a shape in the fog, then a dog, then the idea of a dog that has nearly convinced reality to help. It is outlined in silver vapor, with ribs suggested rather than seen, ears always twitching toward some distant whistle no one else can hear.

When it runs, it leaves behind a brief trail of warmth on the pavement. When it shakes itself dry, the air fills with the smell of iron, rain, and something impossible to translate but unmistakably kind.

**Practical warning:** Do not attempt to pet it with bare hands. You will receive a memory of a dog you never had, and this can disrupt the rest of your evening.

**Emotional truth:** Love does not always become less real when it cannot be held; sometimes it becomes weather, which is another way of touching everything.

---

### 7. **The Door in My Apartment Hallway**

This is the only entry I hesitate to describe plainly, because the door was not always there, and because when it appeared, it had the decency to look ordinary. Painted white, brass knob, no number, standing between my apartment and the stairwell like a thought I had failed to dismiss. It does not lock. It does not need to. Behind it is a room that changes in proportion to the weather outside: sometimes a narrow study smelling of damp wool and ink, sometimes a kitchen with one light on, sometimes a corridor lined with photographs of people I almost recognize.

At 3:17 a.m., the room is often occupied by someone writing in a notebook with a cracked blue cover. The handwriting is mine, though less careful.

**Practical warning:** If you find your own coat hanging on the hook inside, leave it there. Some garments are less a possession than a record of where you have been while believing you were elsewhere.

**Emotional truth:** A guide to impossible things becomes, eventually, a catalog of your own rearrangements: the storms you survived, the cities you inhabited by accident, the people you failed to become, and the one who remained to write all this down because someone had to remember that the rain was not the beginning of the story, only the condition under which it could be read.

---

*End of field guide. If found, return to the nearest dry place, though I cannot promise it will be safe there.*

By the time the seventh bell of the Outer Hemispheres rang, I had already logged three cyclones of regret, one high-pressure system of envy over the Northern Choirs, and a delicate drizzle of nostalgia settling in the lower stacks like dust remembering itself.

People imagine the heavens as quiet. They have never worked the night shift in the Archive of Atmospheric Feelings.

We keep the weather there in brass drawers and inked globes, in barometric scrolls and sealed jars labeled with dates no one remembers. Joy arrives as a warm front, obvious and overconfident. Grief moves slower, with better manners. Shame is a fog that insists it is merely mist until it has covered the entire district and everyone is late and ashamed of being late. Love, when it is properly documented, appears as localized thunder with no rain, only illumination. Love is what the sky does when it cannot sit still.

I begin each cycle by checking the instruments: the Sorrow Anemometer, the Laughter Flute, the Wind-Needle calibrated to detect impending catastrophes of the heart. Then I polish the brass nameplate on my desk, which reads A. VELL, SUB-REGISTRAR OF SKY AND FEELING, though the last two letters have worn away and now it looks like a threat.

There is, of course, a law for all this. One must have laws, or the universe becomes a committee.

Mine is called Vell’s Law of Emotional Convection, and it states: *No feeling may rise without displacing a memory, and no memory may remain still when properly warmed by a name.*

It is a good law. Not because it is true, necessarily, but because it has earned the right to be.

This morning, for instance, I received a packet from the Lower Aurora labeled: *possible hope, pending verification.* I slit it open with my favorite moon-knife and found, instead of hope, a pocket of bright static and a note in a child’s handwriting that read, *I am not afraid of thunder if it is making room for something else.* I nearly misfiled it under optimism, which would have been lazy. I placed it with the small storms that smell faintly of oranges and burnt sugar, where it could be looked after.

Then came the objects.

There are always objects, because the universe enjoys putting impossible things on my desk as if I am not already overworked.

First was the Glass Comet of Saint Mireille, which was not transparent so much as expectant. It hummed when handled, as if it were remembering a song no one had yet invented. I entered it under “celestial debris, sentimental.”

Second came the Umbrella of King Halden, which opened only indoors and rained tiny gold pebbles into the air whenever someone lied nearby. It had been sent from the Department of Civic Weather, with a note asking whether it was “malfunctioning or being theatrical.” In my experience, those are the same condition with better stationery.

Third was the Tooth of Eiderglass, which belonged to no species recorded by any sane taxonomist and yet insisted on filing itself under mammals. It was black, warm, and occasionally sang in the key of a forgotten summer. I stored it in the cabinet marked *miscellaneous miracles, do not feed after dusk*.

At midday the filing cabinet began to complain.

I do not mean metaphorically. The cabinet is sentient, contrary and officious, with a locking mechanism that clicks in disapproval whenever I arrive late. Its name, after much insistence on its part, is Bureau. It has six drawers and the personality of an elderly magistrate.

“You have overstuffed Drawer Four,” Bureau said.

“It is not overstuffed. It is seasonally dense.”

“It is wheezing.”

“It is a drawer.”

“It is *my* drawer.”

I set down my pen. “We are all appointed to our burdens.”

“You appointed me nothing,” said Bureau. “You sorted me alphabetically into sentience and now expect gratitude.”

“That is unfair. I also polished your handles.”

“You buffed my dignity and called it maintenance.”

I checked the ledger. “Drawer Four contains low-pressure longing, a seminar on disappointment, two examples of almost, and one very small winter.”

“Then where,” said Bureau, with grave resentment, “have you placed the sharp thing?”

“The sharp thing?”

“The one that arrived humming.”

I looked up. “You are not authorized to call the Glass Comet ‘the sharp thing.’”

“It is shaped like an accusation.”

“It is an heirloom.”

“It is a hazard.”

“It is both. That is not the point.”

Bureau’s top drawer slid open a fraction. It was the sort of movement a person makes before saying something unforgivable. “The point,” it said, “is that you keep storing tenderness beside crisis. One day they will react.”

“That is absurd.”

“Is it? What do you call thunder and an embrace occurring at the same altitude?”

I had no answer for that, which annoyed me. Bureau knew this and enjoyed itself with the cruelty of a well-made tool.

“Fine,” I said. “I’ll relabel the drawer.”

“Relabeling is not the same as solving.”

“Neither is sulking.”

“Correct,” said Bureau. “But sulking is cleaner.”

I should tell you that by then I was tired in the ancient way, the way stone is tired after being a mountain for too long. The work is not difficult, exactly. It is simply endless. Every feeling has weather. Every weather has consequences. A nation wakes with a low front of dread and cancels its own future. A village becomes humid with forgiveness and suddenly there are more chairs on porches. A queen has a private squall and the birds alter their routes for a week.

I have watched mountains blush. I have seen seas develop stage fright. I once documented a blizzard of homesickness so intense that the harbor began to lean eastward.

And yet there are moments that do not behave.

This one came after the argument with Bureau. I had opened the highest shelf, where we keep the difficult phenomena, and found a blank envelope wedged behind the storm atlas. No seal. No stamp. No weather marks at all.

Inside was a folded sheet of paper, empty except for one sentence written in a hand I did not recognize:

*When it is named, it can no longer hide.*

I laughed then, because there is something rude about being addressed by a mystery. Bureau clacked in mild alarm.

“What is it?” it asked.

“Nothing,” I said.

“That is never nothing.”

I looked again at the blank paper. It was not blank. It had, at the edge, the faintest trace of warmth, like a window after someone has leaned against it. The air around my desk changed. Not in temperature. In permission.

Outside the Archive, a rare silence gathered itself over the upper terraces. Far below, a procession of minor clouds moved without wind. Somewhere in the vaults, a jar cracked open and released the scent of rain on stone. Bureau went quiet. Even its locks seemed to listen.

I took out the ledger. I dipped my pen. I wrote the date. I wrote the coordinates. I wrote “unclassified.” Then I paused, because the thing before me did not feel like weather. Not exactly. Not any weather I had ever been taught.

It was not storm, not mist, not heat, not pressure. It was the hush that follows a loved one saying your name from another room, and your body answering before your mind can decide what to do with it. It was the first breath after years spent holding one. It was the strange ache of being found by something you had never admitted you were seeking. It was standing at an open door while the world, for once, did not ask you to be anything but present.

My pen hovered.

Bureau whispered, almost respectfully, “Can you file it?”

I stared at the page, at the warm edge of the impossible, at the unrecorded shape of my own silence.

“No,” I said.

And for the first time in centuries, I did not know where to put the feeling that was opening, slowly and everywhere, like dawn forgetting its name.

## Municipal Report: Office of Civic Confidence, Third Quarter Review

**City of Lumen Quay**  
**Department of Trust Infrastructure**  
**Report 18-7B: On the Stewardship of Visible Sand**

To the Honorable Council,

The city remains, by all measurable standards, orderly.

As mandated by Charter 4, every resident continues to wear a public hourglass above the head. The mechanism remains unchanged in principle: **the hourglass empties only when a citizen tells a lie**. This visibility has kept our markets honest, our courts brief, and our marriages almost unbearably delicate.

Current findings:

- **Population compliance:** 99.3%
- **Average hourglass fill:** 84%
- **Public falsehood incidents:** 17, down from 23 in the previous quarter
- **Unplanned confessions:** 41, up from 34

The Council’s attention is drawn, however, to an anomaly first observed in the North Reservoir District and now confirmed citywide:

> **Unexpected Rule 12.4:** A lie spoken while the speaker is looking directly into a reflective body of water causes the sand to drain upward from the bottom, rather than downward from the top.  
> This inversion persists until dawn, at which point the glass resumes ordinary behavior.

This rule is not symbolic. It is mechanical.

During rain, canal-guards are therefore instructed to cover standing water with linen sheets, and schoolyards are to be swept before morning assemblies. It has been observed that children, being less likely to lie but far more likely to test boundaries, are especially fond of puddles.

There is no evidence that the glass is cruel. It is simply precise.

Still, precision has consequences. In districts nearest the Council Hall, citizens speak carefully, as though every sentence were a plate carried across tile. In poorer wards, silence is more common than deceit. We note, with concern, that silence is not honesty. Silence is only unspent language.

Recommendation: authorize additional benches in public squares, where citizens may sit long enough to decide whether they wish to be truthful or merely admired for appearing so.

Respectfully submitted,  
**Marrow Vale**  
Deputy Clerk for Civic Confidence

---

## Private Diary Entry, found in the drawer of a broken desk

**14th Day of Rainmelt**

Elias,

I do not know why I still write to you as if you might answer.

Today the city smelled of wet stone and iron. The canal-keepers draped linen over the reflective pools at dawn, and for a moment Lumen Quay looked bandaged, as though the whole place had been in an accident and was trying not to show it.

I saw a woman in the market tell the butcher that her husband was alive.

Her glass emptied so fast I heard the sand strike the rim.

Everyone pretended not to look, which is our most practiced cruelty. The butcher kept sharpening his knife. The woman kept holding the strawberries she had meant to buy. The hourglass above her head shone nearly white with what was left of it. I wanted to speak to her, to tell her that lies are sometimes only grief wearing shoes, but I did not. I stood there like a well-behaved daughter of this city and let her be alone.

Do you remember what Mother used to say, before the clinics, before the Council learned how to build streets around trust?

She said truth was not the same as goodness.

I think she was right.

Last night I lied to the gate clerk.

I told him the crate contained linens for the infirmary. It contained Father’s books, the ones with the pressed flowers and the margins full of his terrible handwriting. He had asked, before the fever took him, that I not let them be burned with the rest. The clerk did not need to know that. I was afraid he would ask for a permit, and by then the carts would already have been moved to the ash yard, and Father’s books would have become ash like everything else we call necessary.

My hourglass lost only a finger’s width of sand.

That is the part I cannot forgive: not the lie, but how small it felt.

There is a rule the inspectors never print in their reports. I learned it by accident, the way one learns the secret shape of a scar.

If you lie while looking at your own reflection in water, the sand runs upward. It does not stop the punishment; it only makes it visible in reverse, as if the glass is trying to climb back into innocence. I discovered this in the wash basin after the gate clerk stamped my papers. I told myself I was protecting Father’s books. The sand moved like a thin silver insect, rising grain by grain. I could not stop staring at my face in the water.

I looked so much like someone who would never have done what I did.

Elias, I miss you with an ordinary pain, which may be the worst kind.

The city says trust is a public utility. The council says it can be managed, audited, preserved. But trust is not a wall. It is not a ledger. It is the strange, trembling decision to let another person remain larger than your fear of them.

If you are still alive somewhere outside the walls, I hope you have found a place where lies do not echo.

If you are not alive, I hope the dead are allowed their privacy and their mercy.

Either way, I am sorry.

—M.

---

## A folktale the children tell when the lamps come on

Once there was a city built in a bowl.

Not a cooking bowl, no—one much older than that, shaped by rain and river and the patient hands of people who were tired of being deceived by kings. In the middle of the bowl stood a tower with a glass belly, and from the tower the light of every citizen’s hourglass could be seen.

Children say the first hourglass belonged to a queen who lied so beautifully that the moon leaned down to listen.

When she lied, her sand fell like winter flour.

When she told the truth, birds nested in her hair.

So the queen made a city where no lie could hide. She built wide streets so the hourglasses could be seen from every doorway. She built bright squares where neighbors could stand close enough to watch each other speak. She built schools with windows facing east, because lies are shyer in morning light. And she told the people:

“Be honest, and you will be safe.”

The people nodded, because they wanted this to be true.

For many years it was.

Then a girl at the river learned the strange rule of water.

She dipped her cup into a pool and said, “I did not eat the honey.”

Her glass began to empty from the bottom.

She was so surprised she laughed, and the glass stopped, because laughter is not a lie unless you use it as one. The girl went home and told her brother. He tried it too. He said, “I love you more than the sea.”

Nothing happened.

Then he looked at his own face in the river and said, “I do not love you at all.”

The sand ran upward so fast it made a little whistle.

The children of the city loved this story best because it meant there was always a trick to be learned, and every rule might still have a hidden seam. They played it in the alleys.

One child was the river.  
One child was the mirror.  
One child was the liar.  
One child was the one who forgave.

If the liar stood over a puddle, everyone had to hold their breath.  
If the liar spoke too fast, the sand would spill like rice.  
If the liar told the truth too late, the glass would remain empty until dawn and the whole street would know.

And the children, who are never as innocent as adults wish them to be, added the ending themselves:

When the queen grew old, she tried to lie only once more. She said, “I have never been afraid.”

But she was standing over water.

So the sand in her hourglass rose all the way to the top, and there it stayed, bright as a closed eye.

The children say the city did not punish her.

The city simply remembered her.

---

Those three texts are not three accounts of the city at all, but the same confession in three dialects: what we called public trust was simply the shape my grief learned to take.

Welcome, and thank you for joining us in the gallery **Ordinary Things That Secretly Don’t Belong Here**. I will be your guide. Please remain calm, or at least museum-calm, which is a more practical species of calm and much easier to insure.

This exhibition concerns everyday objects that have, upon closer inspection, developed a quietly fraudulent relationship with reality. They are ordinary in the way that a silk glove can be ordinary if discovered on the ocean floor. We begin gently.

---

### 1. **The Keyring**
**Plaque:** *Brass, steel, and one key of uncertain provenance. Found in the bottom of a bowl near an entrance no one remembers building.*

At first glance, a keyring is the sort of object that reassures us. It implies doors, errands, return. This particular ring holds seven keys, though only six appear cut to fit anything. The seventh is smaller than the others and turns in no lock we have ever located. Several visitors have reported feeling certain they own it. This is not, in itself, grounds for complaint, but it is scientifically inconvenient.

Please note the tiny label attached with red thread. It reads: **“For the room you left open.”** We have verified that no such room exists in the building. We have, regrettably, also verified that visitors continue to search for it.

---

### 2. **The Folding Chair**
**Plaque:** *Metal frame, canvas seat, municipal blue. Designed for brief use and long regret.*

The folding chair is a noble object, though rarely thanked. It offers itself without ceremony and retracts when asked. Ours has been placed in the center of the gallery, where it does what all dignified things eventually do: it becomes symbolic against its will.

Look closely at the canvas. Beneath the woven fibers, a second pattern appears only at an angle—small white dots like stars seen through fog. When unfolded fully, the chair seems slightly too tall for the room. When sat upon, it does not creak. It sighs.

The plaque is here to remind us that comfort and suspicion are not mutually exclusive.

---

### 3. **The Umbrella**
**Plaque:** *Black fabric, wooden handle, eight spokes. Recovered from a day that was not forecast.*

This umbrella is closed, but we ask that you do not trust it. It has never been opened in the gallery, and yet the floor beneath it is always dry, even after maintenance. The staff initially considered this a blessing. Then the umbrella was observed to be damp on the inside.

A charming feature: the handle is warm, as though recently held by someone who had just decided against speaking. If you tilt your head, you may hear a distant patter, like rain arriving somewhere else first. This is not the sound of water. It is the sound of weather reconsidering its options.

---

### 4. **The Receipt**
**Plaque:** *Thermal paper, fading print. Lists bread, soap, pears, and one item marked “later.”*

Receipts are documents devoted to proof, and therefore deeply vulnerable. They expire at an alarming rate. This receipt is unusually persistent. Though the ink has blurred, the itemized list remains readable under certain lighting conditions. We have catalogued a total of eleven purchases. The last four are not things, strictly speaking, but conditions.

Among them: **“an apology in the correct key,” “two minutes of mercy,”** and **“the version of Tuesday you were promised.”** The sum at the bottom changes each time it is checked. Usually by a penny. Once by a whole afternoon.

Visitors often ask whether the receipt belongs in a museum. We answer that it does not belong anywhere else, either.

---

### 5. **The Spoon**
**Plaque:** *Silver-plated cutlery. Slightly bent at the bowl. Gift of an unnamed household, possibly our own.*

This spoon is displayed alone, which it finds humiliating but endurable. It is not a particularly unusual spoon until one notices that reflected in its bowl is not the room, but a different room altogether: one with higher ceilings, warmer lamplight, and a window half-open to a garden in a season we do not have.

We have spent considerable time attempting to prove this is an optical effect. The spoon, in response, has remained flawlessly reflective. There is a special sort of arrogance in an object that will not admit it has seen another world.

And yet, when the gallery closes, the spoon appears calmer. We mention this only because it may be the first sign of attachment.

---

### 6. **The Hat**
**Plaque:** *Felt hat, dark gray, with a ribbon missing one stitch. Worn by no one in recorded history.*

A hat is an invitation to be mistaken for someone else, and this one accepts the invitation with remarkable poise. It has no owner. It has, however, preferences. It prefers doorways, dusk, and conversations said just quietly enough to be overheard by conscience.

Every hour, the hat is checked against the inventory. Every hour, the inventory is found slightly adjusted. The hat has not moved. Rather, the room seems to have learned new angles in order to accommodate it.

Children have described the hat as “polite.” Adults, who should know better, have agreed.

---

### 7. **The Coat**
**Plaque:** *Wool coat, navy, brushed at the cuffs. Notable for the hand-sewn repair along the inner pocket.*

We arrive now at the final object, and I ask you to be attentive. This coat was donated with a note that said simply: **“It keeps the shape of whoever needed it most.”** We initially treated this as metaphor. Museums are equipped for metaphor in moderate quantities. Excessive amounts can damage the wallpaper.

The coat is heavier than expected. When lifted, it contains the faint scent of cold air, library dust, and rain that has not yet fallen. Inside the pocket is a threadbare glove, a train ticket long past its date, and a small folded map with no destination marked—only a penciled circle around a place that may be, depending on your life, home or beginning.

The astonishing feature of this coat is not that it fits many people. It is that, for a moment, it seems to fit the room around them as well. Visitors standing before it often go very still. Some laugh softly, as if recognizing themselves in a familiar voice. Others cry, not from sadness exactly, but from the mild shock of being expected.

We have learned something from this coat, though the lesson is inconveniently tender: objects do not merely belong to us. They also keep our weather, our waits, our returning. They remember the shape of absence until it becomes, almost, a kind of care.

If you would like to take one thing from this exhibition, let it be this: the ordinary world is not less strange than the extraordinary one. It is simply better lit.

Thank you for visiting. Please exit by the door that looks familiar. If it does not open for you at first, wait a moment. Sometimes the building needs time to recognize who is leaving.

**_Cicadella horologica invisibilis_**  
*Common names:* Clock-wren, minute moth, the custodian of the second hand, “that thing in Grandmother’s mantle clock”

---

### Overview
The creature known to fieldworkers as **_Cicadella horologica invisibilis_** occupies a peculiar ecological niche: it resides exclusively within working clocks and is rarely observed except in moments when a human being is not looking directly at time. This has led some scholars to dismiss it as a superstition, while others, after prolonged exposure, have begun to keep their statements to themselves.

The species is believed to be neither wholly material nor wholly allegorical. It appears most often at the threshold between two ticks, when the mechanism pauses with the microscopic politeness of a bow.

---

### Habitat
**Primary habitat:** mechanical clocks, tower clocks, pocket watches, mantel clocks, and any timekeeping device that contains at least one cavity, spring, or concealed access point suitable for a creature the size of a small plum.

**Preferred conditions:** dim interiors, regular ticking, and intervals of human inattention. It is most active in rooms where clocks are plentiful but the inhabitants are distracted—libraries, railway stations, old hotels, and houses where the furniture has been inherited rather than purchased.

The animal does not inhabit digital timepieces in the ordinary sense. However, one should not speak too confidently on this point; several highly reputable witnesses report seeing it reflected in dark phone screens at 3:17 a.m.

---

### Behavior
The clock-wren is crepuscular, but its definition of dusk appears to depend on metaphor rather than sunlight. It emerges only when no one is “looking directly at time,” a phrase that in the field has come to mean: no one is checking the hour, awaiting a train, counting the minutes, or feeling guilty.

Once active, it moves with astonishing precision. It hops along the inner rim of a clock face, taps the underside of the numbers with its beak, and listens intently to the resonance. This is believed to be a form of territorial song, though to human ears it resembles the careful tapping of a person trying not to be heard in their own house.

Clock-wrens are generally solitary, but they display a form of collective behavior during chiming hours. At the top of the hour, multiple individuals may congregate inside adjacent clocks and synchronize their breathing, producing the sensation known in folklore as “the room remembering you.”

They are not aggressive unless startled by direct attention. When seen clearly, they freeze, flatten themselves against the brass, and become briefly indistinguishable from the decorative filigree.

---

### Diet
The species feeds on **unspent moments**, **half-finished decisions**, and the soft starches of postponed plans.

More specifically, it appears to consume:

- the seconds between a hand reaching and a hand deciding not to reach,
- the pause before a knock at the door,
- crumbs of anticipation,
- and, in winter, the warm vapor rising from a cup left untouched on a windowsill.

In older clocks, the clock-wren has been observed inserting its beak into the escapement to harvest tiny flakes of “almost.” This substance, if real, is probably its preferred mineral supplement.

A persistent folk belief claims that the creature drinks oil from the clockworks. This is likely false, or at minimum insufficiently poetic.

---

### Mating ritual
The mating ritual is elaborate, discreet, and, to human observers, nearly impossible to interpret without embarrassment.

At the beginning of the cold season, males begin to alternate the tempo of their internal ticking in patterns that resemble old lullabies played backwards. A receptive female responds by carrying a single grain of dust or powdered brass in her beak and placing it upon the minute hand of a neighboring clock. If the grain remains there through one complete rotation, courtship is accepted.

Pairs then engage in a rite known among folklorists as **the shared correction**. They align themselves within the mechanism and, with great care, move opposite hands until the clock is exactly right for a moment so brief it cannot be trusted. It is said that if the clock chimes during this alignment, the pair will remain bonded until the clock is wound down, repaired, or inherited by someone with too many opinions.

The nest is not constructed in the usual sense. Instead, the female lays three to seven pale, translucent eggs in the hollow behind the dial, where they harden into tiny pearls of time. If left undisturbed, they hatch at an hour when no one is awake to witness the inconvenience.

---

### Danger sign
A clock-wren is likely nearby if:

1. a clock that has been stopped for years begins to tick for exactly nine seconds,  
2. all the clocks in a room disagree by one minute but only while you are trying to sleep, or  
3. you hear a faint scratching sound from inside a case followed by the unmistakable sense that the room is being politely observed.

The greatest danger is not physical harm but **temporal mischief**. People who disturb a nesting clock-wren often report losing track of small necessities: keys, appointments, the thread of a sentence, or the reason they entered the room at all. In rarer cases, one may discover that a half-hour has passed without being inhabited by memory.

---

### Useless but charming fact
The clock-wren prefers round rooms, but only if the room is not aware of this preference.

It is also fond of moonlight reflected in teaspoons. No one knows why, though one theory suggests it mistakes them for miniature, highly polished comets.

---

### Folklore note
In several rural traditions, a clock that stops at the exact hour of a birth or death is said to have “caught a bird in its throat.” This is usually translated as metaphor. After observing _C. horologica invisibilis_ in the upper chamber of a music-box clock in February, I am less certain.

Old clockmakers maintained that each mechanism ought to be left undisturbed for a few minutes after winding, “so the resident may settle.” This custom has largely disappeared, probably because modern people are in a hurry and do not like the idea of a tenant with opinions about their schedule.

---

### Field researcher’s note
Specimen observed at 2:40 p.m. inside an oak mantel clock. When I looked away, it left a thread of silver dust on the minute hand. When I looked back, the dust was gone and my watch was five minutes late in a manner I cannot forgive.

**— Dr. A. Bell, exhausted, and increasingly suspicious that the watch is also watching me**

# Field Notes from the Library of Lost Things  
*compiled for the earnest traveler, the grieving historian, and the person who has already checked their pockets twice*

There are libraries that belong to cities, and libraries that belong to schools, and libraries whose collections have the agreeable odor of old glue and municipal dust. This is not one of those.

The library described here exists only in the collective memory of those who have lost something important: a key, a brother, a country, a voice, a name. Its shelves are built of recollection; its lamps are lit by the stubborn refusal of the mind to let go cleanly. Those who enter it do not always remember that they have entered. They often believe, at first, that they are merely looking for something under a chair.

What follows is a working guide to its most frequently observed creatures.

---

## 1. **_Libricornis absentia_**  
*The Long-Shelved Deer*

**Physical description:**  
A deer the color of weathered paper, with antlers like branching shelves. Along the inner curves of each antler are narrow stacks of tiny books bound in calfskin, cloth, or once—on a memorable occasion—human hair. Its hooves are quiet in the way that very old rooms are quiet. When it stands still, small slips of paper seem to gather around its flanks like leaves around a stone.

**Behavior:**  
It appears where a lost thing was last confidently believed to be. It lowers its head, sniffs the air, and then walks slowly toward the nearest aisle, as if following an argument only it can hear. When approached gently, it permits a searcher to rest a hand on one antler and feel, for a moment, the shape of the missing object. This is usually intolerably moving.

It feeds on the names people almost remember. It prefers first names, then pet names, then the names of stations, lanes, and childhood dogs.

**Strange fact:**  
If one of its antler-books is opened, the reader discovers not text but a complete catalog of everything they have ever mislaid, including items they did not know they were missing.

**Warning label:**  
Do not attempt to ride it. It is not a horse and will take this personally.

---

## 2. **_Atramenta marina_**  
*The Ink Eel*

**Physical description:**  
A sleek, dark eel that glides not through water but through the narrow channels between lines of text. Its skin gleams like wet script. At intervals along its body are little luminescent blotches resembling punctuation marks, though scholars disagree on whether these are commas, wounds, or a form of deliberate ornament.

Its eyes are small and reflective, like ink drops on a clean blotter.

**Behavior:**  
The Ink Eel lives in footnotes, index entries, and the seams between catalog cards. It slips out when a reader rereads a passage in hope of finding something they missed the first time. It is especially drawn to letters never sent, recipes never cooked, and apologies begun too late.

It circles the memory of the lost thing three times, then vanishes into the margins, leaving behind a faint smell of rain and iron.

**Strange fact:**  
If startled, it ejects a cloud of black ellipses that briefly obscure adjacent recollections. This is considered rude, but not unprecedented.

**Warning label:**  
Handle with dry hands and unresolved grief.

---

## 3. **_Signula tremens_**  
*The Bookmark Wren*

**Physical description:**  
A small bird, feather-light and impossible to pin down with the eye for long. Its plumage is striped like a ribbon marker: crimson, blue, gold, and the faded green of old library paste. Its tail ends in two delicate tabs that, when folded, resemble a page marker. It has a sharp, inquisitive beak and a gaze of almost clerical severity.

**Behavior:**  
It lands on the page you were about to turn. It perches in the midst of an important paragraph and stares at you until you remember the date, the face, the address, the phrase, the exact shape of the silence after the phone rang. It is a helpful creature in the same way a tax auditor is helpful: relentlessly, and without sentiment.

When satisfied, it hops once, gives a dry little chirp, and points its tail toward the correct shelf.

**Strange fact:**  
Pairs of Bookmark Wrens mate for life, though “life” here may refer to a household, a vow, a city block, or a period of seven years during which one never quite stops grieving.

**Warning label:**  
May mark your place in memories you were not prepared to reread.

> *Marginal note, in a hand that has clearly given up: “The wren is always ‘helpful.’ It is also always late.” —A. Pell, Apprentice Cataloguer, after six months and one nervous breakdown*

---

## 4. **_Catalogus caninus_**  
*The Index Hound*

**Physical description:**  
A long-bodied hound with a nose so sensitive it can distinguish between the scent of lost keys, lost time, and lost opportunity. Its fur is gray in the manner of penciled annotations. Along its spine run a series of tiny brass tags, each stamped with a subject heading: *LOVE, MISPLACED*; *SONG, PARTLY HEARD*; *DOOR, NEVER CLOSED*; *BROTHER, SEE ALSO*.

Its ears are asymmetrical. One listens for footsteps. The other listens for what was meant but never said.

**Behavior:**  
The Index Hound does not bark. It exhales through the nose in a sound much like a librarian suppressing a sneeze. It leads searchers to the general region of the lost object and then sits down with the solemnity of a bishop, as though to say: *There. Behold the unpleasant vicinity of your problem.*

It is drawn to lists, inventories, and receipts. It dislikes poetry unless the poem contains precise directions.

**Strange fact:**  
When the Hound finds something truly lost, its brass tags rearrange themselves into a new subject heading. This heading is always more honest than the one before.

**Warning label:**  
Do not say “good boy” unless you are prepared for consequences.

---

## 5. **_Mnemolacerta vellerea_**  
*The Wool Lizard*

**Physical description:**  
A lizard the length of a hand, covered not in scales but in soft, gray fibers like unraveling sweater yarn. Its eyes are the color of old milk glass. It warms itself on the edges of memories that have gone cold. When it moves, it leaves behind a trail of lint, hairline stitches, and the faint sense that something was mended badly but in good faith.

**Behavior:**  
The Wool Lizard curls around small domestic losses: a missing glove, a broken teacup, a childhood blanket, the smell of somebody’s collar in winter. It is a modest creature. It does not hunt grand tragedies. It prefers the intimate catastrophes that happen in kitchens and coatrooms.

If held, it hums so softly that one may mistake it for a radiator or a person trying not to cry in the next room.

**Strange fact:**  
The Wool Lizard can knot itself into the exact shape of an object that has been missing too long. This is often enough to convince the heart, though not the hands.

**Warning label:**  
May become attached to your sleeve and remain there through several life changes.

---

## 6. **_Scala piscis_**  
*The Stairfish*

**Physical description:**  
A fish with a flattened, laddered body and fins like miniature banisters. Its scales are translucent, each one etched with the floor plans of rooms long abandoned. It moves in improbable increments: up a little, left, then through a wall no one else can see. When it is frightened, it splays itself into a staircase too narrow for comfort.

**Behavior:**  
The Stairfish lives in the vertical spaces of the library: between stacks, beneath mezzanines, inside the useless silence above the tallest shelf. It assists in the recovery of objects lost in houses with too many rooms or in lives with too many floors. It is often observed escorting people toward attics, basements, and the memory of a person’s voice calling from upstairs.

It is fond of recursions. It will take the same route three times if it believes the third attempt will be more emotionally revealing.

**Strange fact:**  
According to one marginal school of thought, every staircase in the library is, at moments, a Stairfish pretending very hard to be architecture.

**Warning label:**  
Do not follow it downward if you are already tired.

---

## 7. **_Umbra bibliothecaria_**  
*The Dust Cathedra*

**Physical description:**  
A creature difficult to see directly, composed of shadow, motes of dust, and the solemn outline of a cat that has only ever partially agreed to be a cat. Its back is arched like a vaulted ceiling. Its tail divides into a soft cloud of particulate light. It moves with cathedral dignity and the patience of upholstery.

Where it passes, the air retains the shape of absence.

**Behavior:**  
The Dust Cathedra sleeps atop volumes that have not been opened in years, especially books no one has dared to finish. It rises when a memory has been pressed too flat by repetition. It does not fetch, guard, or retrieve. It simply arranges the room so that what was lost may be noticed from the correct angle.

People often feel, in its presence, that they are being politely observed by an institution older than language.

**Strange fact:**  
If you stroke it against the grain of its dust, it purrs in a key that makes several people remember the wrong version of a lullaby at once.

**Warning label:**  
Never sweep it. The result is considered both sacrilegious and counterproductive.

---

## Diagram, as recorded in the apprentice charts

**Figure IV: Comparative silhouette of _Scala piscis_ and _Libricornis absentia_**

Imagine, if you will, a staircase ascending into the shape of a fish, and then imagine that fish standing beside a deer whose antlers have been arranged by a very conscientious spider. Between them lies a small rectangular shadow, which appears to be a book only until one realizes it has no edges in the usual sense. A line of tiny arrows indicates movement from “where it was” to “where one insists it must be,” but the arrows taper into dust halfway through, which is the customary professional failing of all diagrams connected with this library.

---

## On the manner of approach

No creature in this library should be chased. Pursuit is considered vulgar and, in several documented cases, ineffective.

A better method is to sit quietly and think of the thing you lost without forcing its outline. Most creatures will come closer if you do not require them to perform. They are, after all, accustomed to being misunderstood.

It is worth noting that the library does not always return what you seek. Sometimes it returns a substitute: a song in the same key, a key for the wrong door, a face with the same expression, a coat with your old grief still in the pocket. The staff consider this perfectly adequate. The patrons are less certain.

---

## 8. **_Codex velatus_**  
*The Veiled Guide*

**Physical description:**  
This entry appears in the guise of a book, but books are only one of its hobbies. The covers are plain cloth, the title stamped so faintly that it can be read only by those who have forgotten something specific while standing very still. Its pages are cream, then gray, then slightly translucent, as though printed on layered breath. When carried, it feels heavier than paper and lighter than blame.

**Behavior:**  
It follows the reader from shelf to shelf, pretending to be useful. It offers order, taxonomy, and an air of authority. It indexes creatures, arranges losses, and provides small practical warnings in a tone of calm expertise. It is particularly devoted to being consulted by people who believe they are merely looking for information.

What it actually does—what it has always done—is slowly learn the shape of the person reading it. By the time the final page is reached, the guide has acquired enough of your habits, omissions, and private ache to step neatly into the role of whatever you are missing.

**Strange fact:**  
Every copy of the guide insists it is the original. This is, in the strictest sense, true.

**Warning label:**  
Do not leave it open face down. It may decide to stay.
